case_name: Tehal Singh and Others v State of Punjab
respondent:
State of Punjab
Supreme Court of India

17 October 1978
Cr.A. No. 28 of 1978.
The Judgment was delivered by: CHINNAPPA REDDY, J.
1.  The Tehal Singh was convicted under Section 302, Indian Penal Code on three counts and sentenced to death by the learned Sessions Judge, Faridkot. His brother Darshan Singh and Gurmel Singh were convicted u/s. 302 read with Section 34, Indian Penal Code and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for life. Tehal Singh was also convicted u/s. 27 of the Arms Act and sentenced to suffer imprisonment for three years. The convictions and sentences were confirmed by the High Court of Punjab and Haryana. Tehal Singh, Darshan Singh and Gurmel Singh have appealed to this Court by special leave. Chiman Lal and Murari Lal who were also tried with the three appellants for an offence u/s. 302 read with Section 120-B of the Indian Penal Code were acquired by the learned Sessions Judge. There was no appeal to the High Court against their acquittal.
2
facts: The Tehal Singh was convicted under Section 302, Indian Penal Code on three counts and sentenced to death by the learned Sessions Judge, Faridkot.
There was some rivalry between Chiman Lal and Murari Lal who were transport operators on one side and Pirthi Singh and Harmel Singh, who were also transport operators on the other side.

On August 22, 1976, Pirthi Singh, his brother Harmel Singh, Mithu Singh and Hardip Singh the son of Pirthi Singh, a boy aged 13 years, were returning to their village Giddarbaha from Hussaner in their truck.
Tehal Singh was armed with a double-barrelled gun while Darshan Singh and Gurmel Singh were armed with iron rods.
Pirthi Singh questioned Darshan Singh as to why he had threatened the Munshi of their Truck Union.
There was an exchange of abuse.
Pirthi Singh also slapped Darshan Singh.
Darshan Singh left the scene in a vengeful mood.
Tehal Singh fired a shot which hit Pirthi Singh on the right shoulder, felling him to the ground.
Mithu Singh tried to intervene when Tehal Singh shot at him and killed him instantaneously.
Harmel Singh came forward and be too was shot at by Tehal Singh on the right knee.
He stumbled over a few paces and fell down when Darshan Singh and Gurmel Singh assaulted him with iron rods which were with them.
Tehal Singh then fired a shot into the air and thereafter all the assailants drove away in their truck.
issues: The legal questions or points of law being debated
petitioner_arguments: Dr. Chitale learned counsel for the appellants argued that the dying declaration was a later fabrication, brought into existence by the arrival of Baldev Singh on the scene.
He submitted that the very wealth of detail contained in the dying declaration gave an indication that it was not the statement of the dying man.
He invited our attention to the evidence of the Medical Officer and urged that Harmel Singh would not have been in a position to make the statement attributed to him.
court_reasoning: We do not also see any force in the suggestion of Dr. Chitale that the statement of Harmel Singh was not made in expectation of death and was, therefore, not entitled to weight.

Apart from the fact that S. 32 of the Evidence Act does not require that a statement should be made in expectation of death, it is clear from the evidence that the condition of Harmel Singh was serious at that time.
